1:
The chapter opens by ending something. Ellicott renders the command literally as make to draw near to thee Aaron thy brother, and observes that hitherto the position of Moses had been absolutely unique: from the time Egypt was quitted he had been the one and only intermediary between God and the people, the one and only priest of the nation, and now this was to be changed. He offers two possible reasons, Moses' original want of faith or Aaron's elder birth, and notes that Aaron and his sons were thus drawn near to Moses in rank, position and dignity. Gill takes the same verb as a summons to stand before Moses that he might in the name of the Lord distinguish and separate them. Calvin presses hardest: the calling of God is alleged to prove the dignity of the office, no man taketh this honour unto himself, and among the heathen nations priests were appointed by popular election, so that ambition alone governed their appointment. Not even Christ, he adds, would have been sufficient to propitiate God had he not undertaken the office by the decree of his Father.

That Moses passed over his own family is treated as evidence. Clarke argues from it that Moses cannot have been acting on his own authority, since a man inventing an institution would not have left his own descendants in the condition of ordinary Levites and settled the only dignity in the nation on his brother's house; he adds that the priests had no power of a secular nature, nor does history show them arriving at any until the time of the Asmoneans. Henry reads it as character rather than proof, an instance of the humility of that great man, who was not desirous to engross all the honours to himself and was very well pleased to see his brother invested, remarking that Aaron, who had humbly served as a prophet to his younger brother, is now advanced, for God will exalt those that abase themselves. Wesley repeats the judgement in the same terms and draws the practical reason for a settled priesthood, that those who ministered at the altar had to give themselves wholly to the service.

The four sons are followed forward. Ellicott notes that the actual investiture did not take place until long after the tabernacle was finished, that the office continued in the families of Eleazar and Ithamar, that Eleazar became high priest at Aaron's death and was succeeded by Phinehas, and that at a later date, under circumstances unknown, the high priesthood passed to Ithamar's line, to which Eli belonged. Calvin looks the other way down the same line and finds it vile that the successors of Aaron afterwards bought the priesthood, a traffic Josephus relates, and yet holds that however they violated all law and justice the counsel of God remained inviolable.

The garments are ordered before the work or the consecration. Gill notes that they come first in the account, and that against the shameful practice of some heathen priests who sacrificed naked they covered the man entirely. Ellicott weighs the two stated ends separately: glory, to give the priests an exalted position in the eyes of the nation, and beauty, to establish a harmony between the richly adorned tabernacle and those who ministered in it, concluding that beauty is not a thing despised by the Creator of the universe. Calvin reverses the emphasis, holding that the external ornaments denoted the want of those which are true and spiritual, first concealing Aaron's faults and only then representing the incomparable adornment of all virtues. Clarke turns the verse on his own century, asking whether the dismal black now worn by almost all ministers is for glory and beauty, and whether in zeal against shadows the substance itself is not being changed. Keil begins the description with the ephod, whose etymology he calls uncertain.
3:
Wise hearted is taken as a technical term. Ellicott explains that it means all who had the special knowledge to give effectual aid, and that the Hebrews made the heart the seat of knowledge with perhaps neither more nor less accuracy than underlies our own habit of making it the seat of the affections. Gill reads it as knowledge in mechanic arts, and notes that these were uncommon garments requiring more than ordinary skill, thought and judgment to make exactly. Ellicott then meets an objection, granting that few passages are more antagonistic to modern thought than God speaking of himself as having infused his Spirit into men in order to enable them to produce satisfactory priestly garments; his replies are that God is the fountain of all knowledge, that he alone knows what is beneath him, and that dress is not insignificant or so much would not have been said in Scripture about it.

Clarke turns the same clause into a general doctrine of genius. Ingenuity in arts and sciences, even the ornamental kind, comes from God; the direction to Moses was to select those he found expert, and the words show that such men had derived their knowledge from God himself. No man, he insists, ever acquired a genius of this kind by course of reading or study; we call it natural and say it was born with the man, but Moses teaches us to consider it divine. He names Napier inventing the logarithms, Copernicus and Kepler pulling down the false systems of the universe and Newton demonstrating the true one, and answers that no reading, no study, no example formed Newton's genius. He appeals to the ploughman whom his God doth instruct to discretion. Then he checks himself twice: machinery is to help man, not render him useless, the human hand being the most perfect machine, and in our zeal for it the land is filled with beggary and the workhouses with paupers.

The list of six garments is handled philologically. Clarke derives the robe from a root meaning to go up, so that it may be considered an upper coat or surtout, and cites Josephus that it reached to the feet and was one entire garment woven throughout rather than made of two pieces. The broidered coat he gives from Parkhurst as a close, strait garment, and from Josephus as a tunic closely encompassing the body with tight sleeves, answering the purpose our shirts answer to us. The mitre he traces to a root meaning to roll or wrap round, making it the turban so universal in eastern countries, and suggests that the Persian word behind our turban compounds elements meaning a revolution and to bind, with Hebrew roots possibly behind those. The girdle he takes as the common eastern sash that confined the loose garments at the waist and in which the long skirts were tucked up for work or a journey.

Ellicott arranges rather than derives. He observes that the high priest's garments are taken first and described through thirty six verses, that the breastplate is mentioned first as most conspicuous, that the ephod was a sort of jerkin or waistcoat on which it was worn, and that under it lay the long blue robe, the main garment; he adds that nothing is said of any covering for the feet, though sandals are probable. The materials, he notes, are those used for the vail and curtains of the sanctuary, with gold and precious stones added. Gill adds from the Targum of Jonathan that the makers took not out of their own substance but received from Moses what the people had freely offered. Calvin, before any of this, warns his readers to abandon all subtle speculations and be contented with simplicity, since he could repeat many plausible allegories that some would favour above a sound knowledge of facts.
6:
The shape of the ephod is disputed at every measurement. Gill sets the rabbinic authorities against one another: it reached to the loins per Kimchi, or the buttocks per Abarbinel, and not to the feet as Jarchi and Maimonides held, since Josephus makes it a cubit, little more than half a yard. The hinder part covered the back, the forepart the breast and belly, buttoned with onyx stones at the top of the shoulders and girt with the curious girdle; and he contradicts Josephus again, holding it had no sleeves, as appears from the make of it. Henry and Wesley agree that it was the outermost garment, a short coat without sleeves, and both call it the golden ephod for the gold woven into it, distinguishing it from the plain linen ephods worn by inferior priests, by Samuel as a child and by David dancing before the ark.

Keil argues the construction against a named opponent. Comparing the parallel account of the making, he holds there can hardly be any doubt that it consisted of two pieces connected at the top over the shoulders, and that Knobel is wrong to suppose a single piece with a hole cut each side for the arms. His argument is from silence used carefully: if it had been a compact garment which had to be drawn over the head like the robe, the opening for the head would certainly have been mentioned, as it is in the case of the robe. He takes the text to point most decidedly to the rabbinical idea, two pieces reaching to about the hip, one over the breast and the other down the back. Gill describes the same shoulder pieces as running from the arm holes on both sides, coming from before and behind and meeting to be buttoned there. Ellicott corrects only the article, preferring simply two shoulder pieces.

The curious girdle is a translation problem before it is an object. Clarke observes that the word so rendered signifies merely a kind of diaper or embroidered work, widely different from the word properly translated girdle in the list; two consequences are drawn from this, that the connecting pieces at the shoulders were of the same texture as the ephod, or that some girdle is meant differing from the other in being only of plain workmanship. Ellicott agrees that the word means properly device or ornamental work and does not itself mean belt, but sees no reason to doubt the thing was a girdle, since Josephus calls it one and describes it as dyed of many hues with gold interwoven, the name taken from the skill displayed in its patterning; of the same he explains as woven continuously with the front or back piece, not sewn on. Keil traces the word instead to a root meaning to bind or fasten, so that it is properly a girdle and not, as the Greek version and others took it, a weaving.

Henry and Wesley read the garment forward. Christ the high priest appeared to John girt about with a golden girdle such as the curious girdle of the ephod; righteousness is the girdle of his loins, and he is girt with strength for the work of our salvation. The government is said to be upon his shoulders as Aaron had the names of all Israel there in precious stone, and he presents to his Father a glorious church, having power to support them and interest to recommend them. Henry adds that he bears them before the Lord for a memorial, in token of his appearing before God as the representative of all Israel and an advocate for them. Gill reaches the same destination by a shorter route, taking the ephod as a symbol of the human nature of Christ.
9:
Nobody is sure what stone is meant. Gill lists the disagreement without settling it: the name is taken from the colour of a man's nail, Onkelos, Jonathan and the Syriac make it beryl, the Greek version emerald, the Arabic crystal, and Josephus sardonyx, which Braunius thought right. Ellicott reaches the same shortlist and decides it on technical grounds. Some have taken the Hebrew word for emerald and others for beryl, but it is probably the onyx or the variety known as sardonyx, a stone of three layers, black, white and red; the decisive consideration is that emeralds could not have been cut by any process known at the time, while onyx and sardonyx served early as signet stones in Egypt and elsewhere.

The engraving is defended as historically possible. Ellicott observes that gem cutting was practised from a remote antiquity in Egypt and Babylonia, that the best Assyriologists place Chaldaean signet cylinders at least two thousand years before Christ and Egyptian signets reach the twelfth dynasty, and that while the hardest stones defied the art of the time, stones of the second class readily yielded to the engraver's tools. He adds that there is no difficulty in supposing that among the Israelites were men who had worked in Egyptian workshops during the servitude. Clarke claims a debt: engraving on precious stones was carried in antiquity to a pitch of perfection never since rivalled, particularly among the Greeks, and it is very likely the Greeks borrowed the art from the Hebrews, since it flourished in Egypt and Palestine long before it was known in Greece.

The arrangement raises an arithmetical difficulty nobody solves. Keil takes according to their generations to mean by their respective ages, and follows Josephus in putting the six elder sons on the right shoulder and the six younger on the left; Gill says the same. Ellicott states the problem the twelve names create, that either Levi was omitted or Joseph replaced Ephraim and Manasseh, and leaves both standing. On the settings the two lexical accounts collide. Clarke derives the word rendered ouches from a root meaning to close or enclose, makes it strait places or sockets, and says flatly that socket is the proper translation since ouch cannot be traced up to any legitimate authority. Ellicott traces it to a legitimate authority: more properly nouch, from the old French for a buckle or clasp, citing Skeat. Wesley describes the thing rather than the word, hollow places such as are made in gold rings to hold the stones, and Ellicott adds that these rosettes of open work must have been sewn on. Keil notes that the chains were not formed of links but of gold thread twisted into cords.

What the memorial is for divides them. Keil argues from the shape of the garment: the burden of office rested on the shoulder and its insignia were worn there, so engraving the tribal names there showed that the high priest brought the nation to God as mediator. Ellicott corrects the preposition, reading not a memorial to the children of Israel but for them, the stones reminding God that the priest represented all the tribes and pleaded in their name. Clarke says the same while flagging the anthropomorphism, that speaking after the manner of men God was to be put in mind of the children of Israel as often as the high priest appeared before him. Calvin canvasses three readings, that God may be mindful of them, that the priest may remember them, or that they may remember God is reconciled, and takes none, interpreting simply a monument of the mutual agreement. His own emphasis falls elsewhere: the engraving removed all occasion of envy, since the people would understand that this man was not separated for private advantage but that in him they were all a kingdom of priests.
15:
The title is explained three ways. Ellicott denies that the Hebrew word means breastplate at all, giving ornament, and says it is called the ornament of judgment because it held the Urim and Thummim, by which God's judgments were made known. Clarke keeps the name but grounds it in practice, the priest wearing it to ask counsel of the Lord and to sit as judge, teaching the law and determining controversies. Gill makes it admonitory, a reminder that he should do justice, have at heart the judgment of the people, and in hard cases ask it of God and faithfully declare it. Henry proposes reading the later command as give, or add, or deliver to the breastplate the illuminations and perfections, so that no new object need be made at all.

The dimensions raise a structural question. Clarke gives it as a span square when doubled and so two spans long before, and supposes the Urim and Thummim were placed between the folds; Gill reports from Maimonides that the length was a cubit, two spans, so that doubled it was one. Ellicott reckons the span at about nine inches and argues the doubling was structural: Symmachus renders the word a receptacle or bag, and material objects to be put inside would make such a construction necessary, since doubling was not needed for strength alone, linen corselets stout enough to resist a sword being among the manufactures of Egypt. He adds that the square carries the idea of perfection, and that but for this twelve gems would suit an oblong.

The stones themselves resist identification, and both the men who try say so. Gill works through them and keeps meeting pairs that can be swapped: the second row's first stone is emerald in both Targums, carbuncle in the Greek, ruby in Braunius and Abarbinel, and he cites De Dieu's rule that whoever renders the preceding stone an emerald must render this a carbuncle, and the reverse. He derives the ligure from the congealed urine of the lynx, or rather from that creature's spots, since Danaeus identifies it with the stellina, named from the star-like specks spread through it; he notes that the agate, now of little account, was formerly esteemed, Pyrrhus of Epirus owning one in which the nine Muses and Apollo with a harp appeared by nature and not by art; and he takes the fourth row to open with a sea-green stone because the word behind it means the sea.

Clarke tabulates all twelve against the sons in birth order after the Jerusalem Targum and Ainsworth, and reports that Jonathan set the four rows opposite the four quarters of the world, objecting that this could hold only if the thing lay flat and not when it hung on the priest's breast. He then withdraws his own confidence: he cannot say the stones he has described are precisely those intended, nor assert that the tribes are arranged exactly as Moses meant, since these things are not laid down so as to preclude mistake and some must be left to conjecture; and he has omitted the fabulous accounts given by ancients and moderns alike, and the spiritual meanings others find so plentifully in each stone, as puerile, futile, and not a few dangerous. Ellicott insists on twelve, neither more nor fewer, each stone standing for one tribe. Gill reports and rejects the suggestion that Levi's name was omitted; Henry and Wesley leave both possibilities open, that Levi had no stone and Ephraim and Manasseh were reckoned distinct as Jacob had said, or that Levi had one and the two were one in Joseph. Keil observes that the gold borders round the settings not only ornamented the stones but helped fix them more firmly. Henry adds that the ephod was the garment of service and the breastplate an emblem of honour, and that these two must by no means be separated.
22:
The chains are described by what they are not. Gill reports the Targum of Jonathan rendering them chains of a certain determined size, of length and thickness exactly alike, or as he alternatively puts it terminable ones, not circular like a locket or a chain worn about the neck but having ends; and he notes that some interpret them as made like ropes, twisted together in the manner of cables, which he thinks the following verses put beyond doubt. Ellicott offers the same two possibilities as competing renderings, chains of equal length or chains of wreathen work, and gives the Hebrew literally as after the manner of ropes. Keil treats the whole verse as redundant, holding that it simply repeats the earlier command, and argues the point twice over: the chains are mentioned only once in the later account of the work actually executed, and the instruction that follows fastens them on the same rosettes already described.

Three pairs of rings are ordered, and the commentators spend their effort keeping them apart. Gill counts them as they come, the first pair set on the upper part of the breastplate toward the shoulder pieces to receive one end of the chains, the second pair a distinct set, and the third pair not for the breastplate at all but for the ephod. Ellicott places the first pair on the two upper corners and explains that the chains were passed through them and then united with the settings of the ephod; the second pair he puts on the two lower corners, in the border, at its extreme edge. Keil describes the second pair as set at the ends of the breastplate on the side turned inward toward the ephod, and the third upon the shoulder pieces underneath, toward the front, near the joining above the girdle. Gill adds a guess about the attachment at the top, that there were probably rings on the settings into which the far ends of the chains were put, or that they were by some means fastened to them.

The blue lace is given a mechanical purpose. Keil explains that the lower rings of the breastplate were tied to the lower rings of the ephod with threads of hyacinth so that the breastplate might keep its place above the girdle and against the ephod without shifting, and he glosses the verb behind the phrase not loosed as meaning to move away or be removed. Gill records a different construction of the same verb, that some take it as lift up, so that the sense would be that they should lift the breastplate to join it with the ephod above it.

The last verse is read as the point of all the hardware. Ellicott takes the two placements together: the high priest was to be wholly identified with the people, one with them in affection no less than in action, bearing their names on his shoulders as supporting them and wrestling for them while he bore their names on his heart as loving them and feeling for them, so that he continually presented a twofold memorial and made a sort of double appeal, on the one hand to God's power and on the other to his mercy and loving-kindness. Keil states it more briefly, that Aaron was to bear the names engraved upon the breastplate as a memorial before the Lord whenever he went into the sanctuary. Gill turns representation into a history: the twelve tribes were represented in eternity and in time, in the sufferings and death of Christ, in his burial and resurrection when they were crucified, buried and raised with him, and now in heaven, where they sit together in heavenly places in him.
30:
Everyone begins by admitting the difficulty. Gill says interpreters Jewish and Christian alike are at a loss, some confessing plain ignorance, and lists the guesses: that they were these two words written and placed in the fold, that the divine name was put there, that they were little images like the teraphim carried in the folds and consulted, or that they were a work purely divine of God's own putting. He then takes a side, following Josephus in identifying them with the twelve stones, and argues from distribution: where the stones are mentioned nothing is said of the Urim and Thummim, and where these are named no notice is taken of the stones. Clarke opens flatly, that what these were has never yet been discovered, and numbers his reasons: they are nowhere described, no direction is given how to make them, and they do not appear to have been made here, so that if they were man's work at all they were articles already in use, undescribed because well known.

Ellicott builds the opposite case. He argues materiality on three grounds: the phrase is identical with that for putting the two tables into the ark and can scarcely mean anything but placing one thing inside another; the words carry the article at their first mention, as though already familiar; and Philo and Josephus, who differ in every other respect, agree that material objects are meant. He then removes both ancient answers. Philo's two sides of the breastplate fail because those were not put in after it was complete, and the twelve jewels fail because the passage distinguishes them from the stones. What remains is small objects the bag could hold and the people had long known; and here, he says, the greatest difference appears: cut and uncut diamonds, metal slips marked yes and no, lots, and small images like the teraphim. He judges certainty unattainable, inclines to the images on the strength of a connection with older divination, and says how the consultation was made and the answer given admits of no solution at all.

Two textual points cut against the consensus. Clarke reports that the Samaritan text adds a clause absent from the Hebrew, thou shalt make the Urim and the Thummim, granting that if admitted it would mean they were manufactured here like everything else. He also cites Rabbi Menachem, that they were no artificer's work and neither artificers nor congregation had any work or offering in them, but they were a mystery delivered to Moses from the mouth of God. Keil insists on the preposition: the phrase always means putting one thing into another and never suspending one upon another, so that against Knobel they were distinct from the breastplate and placed inside it, the Greek version's upon notwithstanding.

The names are read as a programme. Clarke takes lights and perfections to point to the information in spiritual things afforded under the law and the holiness that dispensation required, noting that the Latin gives doctrine and truth and the Greek manifestation and truth, and that no version supposes anything material is intended. He adds from Diodorus that the president of the Egyptian courts wore a golden chain carrying an image set with precious stones called Truth, turned toward the party whose cause was found just. Calvin, reporting the same two options Gill weighed, thinks nothing more probable than that the breastplate itself represented light in doctrine and uprightness of life, and reads the judgment of the children of Israel as a defined system, an absolutely perfect rule to which they ought to conform. Keil makes the connection structurally, that the thing was called the breastplate of judgment precisely because these were in it, bringing the right of Israel before the Lord. Wesley calls them the high priest's cabinet council under a theocracy, and records that the oracle was lost in the captivity and never retrieved.
31:
The robe is defined against the ephod. Keil calls it an upper garment of dark blue purple, and warns against imagining a cloak: it was a long closely fitting coat reaching only to the knees, so as to show the coat underneath, not to the feet as the Alexandrian rendering suggests. Gill agrees it was longer than the ephod and worn under it, but of different materials, linen only and wholly blue without the figures worked on the other. He presses the seamlessness: it was woven from top to bottom, and Josephus says it was not two parts nor sewed at shoulder or side but one long piece of woven work. From this he draws the comparison with the seamless coat Christ wore, both an emblem of a righteousness with nothing of men's works joined to it; the garment's name, he adds, comes from a word signifying prevarication, because it covers the sins of God's people. Henry and Wesley add that it was sleeveless and drawn on over the head, with side holes for the arms, or per Maimonides not sewed at the sides at all. Clarke, following Josephus, makes it one long straight piece with an opening in the centre for the head.

The reinforced neck-opening is a small archaeological question. Keil explains that the hem round it was weavers' work, like the opening of the habergeon, that it be not torn, and takes the habergeon to be the linen corselet Ajax wears in the Iliad, noting from Hengstenberg that Egypt made these artfully. Ellicott thinks the Hebrew word for habergeon Egyptian; Wesley glosses it a coat of armour.

The trimming points away from Egypt. Ellicott observes that the pomegranate was an Assyrian favourite and not Egyptian, and reasons that Babylonian fabrics reaching Syria not much later probably circulated in Egypt too. The bell he finds more foreign still: more Assyrian than Egyptian, without direct parallel as priestly costume, unknown in the religious services of any ancient nation, and the claim that Persian kings wore them resting on no sufficient authority, so that an entirely new religious usage seems to be introduced here. Keil reports Rashi's description of the pomegranates as round globes about the size of hens' eggs, and derives the word for bell from a root meaning to strike, which settles that a bell and not a spherical ball is meant. Gill notes only that the two alternated.

The purpose of the sound divides practical from figurative. Ellicott makes it corporate: the great object was to publish every movement of the people's representative, so that they could follow the service in thought and offer a common worship, a union held so important that death was denounced on a priest ministering without the garment. Henry and Wesley say the bells gave notice to those in the outer court when he went in to burn incense, that they might pray at the same hour in concurrence with him. Clarke adds a court custom: God appeared in the tabernacle as an emperor in his tent among his troops, and at the doors of eastern grandees some sonorous body was struck to announce that a person sought admittance; the tabernacle having only a veil, the bells served that office. Keil cites the later explanation that the noise was a memorial, and Hiskuni's gloss that the people might know the hour of service. Calvin allegorises and defends doing so: pomegranates have no smell, yet the type suggested one to the eye, as if God required a savour as well as a sound; and we who stink through the foulness of our sins are sweet to God only as covered with the garment of Christ, which procures favour solely by the sound of the Gospel. He insists nothing in this is far-fetched, and quotes Gregory that the priest is worthy of death from whom the voice of preaching is not heard.
36:
What the plate looked like is inferred from the word. Clarke notes that the term rendered plate means a flower and the Greek gives a leaf, suggesting a wreath; since it is elsewhere called a crown, and the Jewish author of Wisdom a diadem, he thinks it shaped less like the ancient diadem than like the radiated crown of the Roman emperors, though worn round the forehead. Keil derives the word from a root meaning to shine, notes that it is called the crown of holiness, and places it on a dark blue riband above the lower coil of the head-band, whose own name comes from a root meaning to twist and is used of no one but the high priest. Gill reports from Jarchi and Maimonides that it was two fingers broad and reached from ear to ear, which the Targum of Jonathan puts as from temple to temple. Ellicott makes it the essence of the mitre, put forward first as that whereto all the rest is subordinate and catching the eye more than the breastplate.

The inscription is treated as script as well as sense. Clarke holds it allowed on all hands to have stood in the primitive Hebrew character seen on ancient shekels, and observes that the divine name in it is the word of four letters the Jews will to this day neither write nor pronounce; he adds their tradition that the letters were embossed rather than cut, and that the plate sat between the hair and the eyebrows. Wesley insists on the manner of the engraving, deep and durable like a signet, not painted so as to be washed off. Ellicott looks past the metal: the plate was only the vehicle of an inscription, and what it taught was that religion culminates in holiness to the Lord, without which forms, ceremonies, priestly attire, sacrifice and prayer are mockeries; and it was a call not to the priest only but to the whole nation. Calvin explains the placing: it stood on the forehead to be conspicuous, testifying both that the priesthood of God's appointment pleases him and that holiness was not to be sought elsewhere.

The last clause is the one they all reach for. Ellicott identifies the holy things as the people's offerings, always carrying some imperfection owing to the imperfection of human nature and the mixed character of human motives; the priest's official holiness let him present them without offending God, and was accepted as purging them of their impurity. Clarke translates the verb as bearing in a vicarious and typical manner, notes that the same verb is used of the servant in Isaiah, and draws out the doubling: Aaron atoned not only for the people's sins but for the imperfection of the atonement itself.

Calvin calls it a remarkable passage and works it hardest. He rules out the easy reading, that this concerns gross sins, whose pardon is plainly to be had only through Christ; what is cleansed is the iniquity of the holy oblations. He rejects as a poor exposition the view that only errors in the ceremonies were remitted by the priest's prayers, since no offering, so far as it is of man, is altogether free from guilt. He concedes the harshness of this, that our very holinesses need pardon, and illustrates it: water drawn pure from a limpid fountain is made turbid passing over muddy ground, and nothing is so pure as not to be polluted by the contagion of our flesh. The conclusion is that whatever good works we strive to present to God are so far from deserving reward that they rather convict us of guilt, unless the holiness of Christ obtains pardon for them. Wesley states it more simply, that Christ bears this iniquity for us so as to bear it from us. Gill, keeping to the object, calls the plate a priestly crown.
39:
Ellicott marks the transition and quarrels twice with the translation. The garments described so far have been the outer ones, and now the inner are added, of which there was but little to be said: linen drawers, a linen tunic woven in a peculiar way, and a girdle to confine it. The verb rendered embroider he reports to be generally agreed wrong, Kalisch giving weave, Gesenius work in chequer and Cook weave in diaper work, the Hebrew being a rare word for some particular kind of weaving. Coat he calls unfortunate too: the thing was a long white linen tunic with tight sleeves reaching nearly to the feet, and the sleeves must have shown, being the only covering of the priest's arms. The girdle's colours, he notes, were needle-worked rather than woven, and since it was worn above the tunic and under the robe little of it could have been seen, though perhaps the ends hung below.

Gill canvasses three accounts of the tunic's texture. Some make it full of eyelet holes; Jarchi supposes holes like the sockets that held the stones, so that the coat was decked with gems set into them; Gill prefers the third, that it was figured with the small cornered cells of a ruminant's stomach, network in form, which he takes from Maimonides and finds approved by Braunius. Wesley says only that it reached to the feet and the sleeves to the wrists and was bound with a girdle of needlework, and takes the linen mitre to be such as kings anciently wore in the east, typifying the kingly office of Christ.

The ordinary priests get the same articles, plainer. Keil observes that their dress had the same items as Aaron's, but their body-coat is called weavers' work and was therefore plain white byssus, whole throughout and without seam like the robe of Christ, worn close to the body and reaching, on Jewish tradition and Josephus, to the ankles. Their head-dress he derives from a word for a cup, so that it seems to have been an inverted cup in form, a plain white cotton cap. Ellicott agrees and raises the difficulty: it is certainly remarkable that so plain a dress, a white tunic, a girdle perhaps embroidered, and a close-fitting cap, should suffice for glory and for beauty. His answer is that white robes are in Scripture constantly represented as eminently glorious. Henry notes only that their bonnets differed in shape from the high priest's mitre, and turns the phrase against itself: all this glory was nothing to the glory of grace, and this beauty nothing to the beauty of holiness the garments typified.

The consecration is read through one idiom. Calvin takes up the phrase about filling their hands: they are filled when the men are made fit to offer sacrifices, since unconsecrated hands are accounted empty even though they may be very full, no gift being acceptable to God except in right of the priesthood. He presses that it is Moses and not their father Aaron who sanctifies them, so that the power may rest in God and not be transferred to his ministers; and he suggests God was forestalling the calumnies of the ungodly, lest anyone object that Aaron had extended to his sons an honour conferred on himself alone. In inaugurating Aaron's children, he adds, Moses reduced his own to their proper place. Keil makes the same distinction between office and person: because the dress was official, Moses was to put it on them, anoint them and fill their hands, and although the office's holiness was reflected in the dress, their sinful nature required a special consecration besides. Gill treats the vesting itself as the act, the putting on of the garments by Moses under God's authority being a solemn investiture, since from that point they might exercise the office and might never officiate without them.
42:
Keil notices that these last two verses stand apart and explains why. Covering nakedness was an indispensable prerequisite rather than an ornament, so its directions are separated from those about the portions of the dress that were for glory and beauty. He derives the Hebrew name from a root meaning to conceal, so that the things are literally concealers, short drawers from the hips to the thighs. Their material he leaves open: the word is uncertain, the parallel makes it byssus or cotton yarn, and the Greek rendering of linen is no obstacle, since the ancients applied their word for flax to fine white cotton too; probably it was a white cloth, from a root meaning to be clean. Ellicott corrects the English to drawers and adds that such garments, from the waist to a little above the knee, were the sole garment of many in Egypt and a necessary garment of all.

The reason given is decency, and each man names a different threat to it. Gill takes the phrase as the flesh of nakedness, that part which when exposed causes shame and ridicule, and generalises that great care was taken in God's house to preserve decency, prevent immodesty and guard against laughter and levity. Calvin states the principle behind the precept: since men in their natural levity seize the slightest causes of offence to the disparagement of holy things, so that religion easily sinks into contempt, God commands an apparently trivial matter as a precaution, the sum being that the priests should conduct themselves chastely lest anything indecorous impair the majesty of holy things. Clarke looks outward instead, finding the command aimed at the shocking indecency of the pagan worship in general, in which the priests often ministered naked, as in the sacrifices to Bacchus.

Clarke then states a rule for the chapter. There can be no doubt, he says, that the garments were emblematical of spiritual things, but of which, and in what way, no man can positively say; commentators have entered largely into it and made edifying remarks, yet where no clue guides us through a labyrinth in which mistake is possible at every moment, it is much better not to be wise above what is written, since reflections not clearly deducible from the text give little satisfaction to a sincere inquirer. He will allow four general senses: purity in every part of divine worship, the necessity of an atonement for sin, the purity and justice of the divine majesty, and the absolute necessity of that holiness without which none can see the Lord.

The threat and the perpetuity close the chapter. Keil takes bearing iniquity and dying as incurring guilt deserving death, whether by disobedience or, what he thinks weightier, by violating the reverence due to the holiness of God's dwelling; and he reasons that since the consciousness of sin first showed itself in the feeling of nakedness, those members are especially objects of shame. Gill extends the requirement to all the garments and not the drawers only, and reports the Targum of Jonathan's specification that the death would come by fire from heaven, such as afterwards consumed Nadab and Abihu. Ellicott identifies the holy place here with the court, notes that death is threatened for ministering without these garments as it was for neglecting the robe, and judges that in both cases a divine vengeance rather than a legal punishment is probably intended. Calvin objects that some improperly restrict the perpetual statute to the breeches alone when it refers naturally to the other ordinances, and argues that the perpetuity attains its end in Christ, these figures being established precisely because their use ceased once their reality appeared, the priesthood being transferred and the law with it. Wesley says the same in a sentence, that it lasts as long as the priesthood and has its perpetuity in the substance of which these were the shadows.
